Copying DNA began on a night drive. In California in 1983, Kary Mullis, a chemist at Cetus, saw how to copy one piece of DNA.

Heat splits the two strands. Cool it, and short starters attach. An enzyme builds the missing halves. Repeat, and the copies double: 30 rounds make over 1 billion copies. Early on the heat killed the enzyme, so it was added fresh each round, until a heat-loving bacterium's enzyme survived and machines ran the rounds alone. The method was published in 1985, and Mullis shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Every virus test and forensic DNA match starts with it.

Builders wanted. The Ad Astra Fellowship: 12 months, a room, food, the labs, the machine shop and the compute at $0, a company in your name from day 1. 1 written application, no credentials needed. Apply at joinadastra.com
